title: Salt (Mark 9:42–50)
hook: have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another

segments.voice: Yesterday, John tried to stop a stranger, and heard forbid him not. Your line was not against us, for us.

Still in the same house, with the friends who argued about rank, Jesus says some of the hardest-sounding things in Mark. Whoever trips up one of these little ones who believe, better for them to have a millstone hung around their neck and be thrown into the sea. If your hand makes you stumble, cut it off. If your foot, cut it off. If your eye, pluck it out. Better to enter life missing a part than, in the King James words, to be cast into hell fire. Church tradition reads them as deliberate exaggeration, not instructions. Then, right at the end, the tone changes, and he talks about something on every kitchen table.
screen: `A MILLSTONE AND THE SEA.` → `CUT IT OFF.` → `SOMETHING ON EVERY TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another." Salt was precious. Before refrigerators, it kept fish and meat from rotting, and it gave taste. In the Hebrew Bible, offerings were seasoned with salt, and there's a phrase, a covenant of salt, for a promise meant to last. Can salt really lose its saltness? Pure salt can't. Some readers suggest the salt people used then was mixed with other minerals, so damp could wash the true salt out and leave white stuff that tasted of nothing. Just before comes a line nobody is sure about: "every one shall be salted with fire." Mark doesn't explain it; readers still puzzle. The ending is clear: salt in yourselves, and peace with one another. He's talking to the men who argued about rank and shut out the stranger. One way to hear it: keep your taste, your bite. Just don't turn the bite on each other. That closes this stretch of Mark, the one that kept asking who is this. Washed hands and what comes out of the heart. Crumbs for a mother's daughter. Be opened. Seven baskets. Hard hearts in a boat. Men like trees. You are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. Help my unbelief. Who's the greatest. Not one of us. And salt. Tomorrow the road turns south, toward Jerusalem.
screen: `SALT KEPT THINGS AND GAVE TASTE.` · `SALT THAT LOSES ITS SALTNESS.` · `SALTED WITH FIRE: NOBODY'S SURE.` · `SALT IN YOU, PEACE WITH EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `HAVE SALT IN YOURSELVES, AND HAVE PEACE ONE WITH ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you're a little crossways with right now, nothing huge: a sharp text, a cold week, a silence that went on too long. Keep your salt, you don't have to pretend you were wrong about everything, but ask what one step toward peace would look like: a message, a kind word, letting it go. If you pray, bring them to God by name.
Salt. It keeps things and gives them taste. Have salt in yourselves, he says, and have peace one with another.
Your line: salt, and peace. Keep your bite, and keep the peace. Day one hundred ninety-nine, done.

howItsDone: Christians often speak of being "the salt of the earth" and read Mark 9:50 as a call to keep their faith lively and to make peace within the church; in some congregations people share the peace, a greeting or handshake, during worship.
